I'm Vandana, and I sit two benches behind Lokesh in Class 10. When Priyanka's new calculator went missing after the maths period, I was sure it was him.
Ma'am asked everyone, "Did anyone take it?" Lokesh went red, looked at the floor and kept pulling at his collar. He couldn't even meet her eyes. Liar, I thought. Obviously.
Meanwhile Jatin, sitting beside him, looked straight at Ma'am and said calmly, "No, Ma'am. I didn't see it."
At the end of the day, the calculator fell out of Jatin's bag when he pulled out his water bottle.
I sat there feeling stupid. Lokesh, it turned out, goes red whenever a teacher looks at him, about anything. Later I heard him say to a friend, "I always look guilty. I hate it."
I had been so sure. I had been completely wrong.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do when Ma'am asked the class?
qa.a: Lokesh went red, looked at the floor and kept pulling at his collar.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel when the calculator fell out of Jatin's bag?
qa.a: Vandana felt stupid and ashamed, realising the nervous signs had fooled her completely.

qa.q: What could Vandana do next time she suspects someone?
qa.a: She could wait for real evidence instead of reading nervousness as guilt, and remember that calm faces can hide lies too.

qa.q: How does Lokesh feel about the way he reacts?
qa.a: Lokesh feels frustrated and embarrassed, hating that he always looks guilty even when he is innocent.

grounding: A classmate observes that nervous signs like avoiding eye contact were wrongly read as lying, while the calm student was the one who took it.

Sunday. Pooja found her headphones on the floor of her room, one earpiece snapped off. Her little brother Chetan was in the doorway. When she asked, he looked at the ceiling and fidgeted with his shirt. "I didn't touch them." Pooja was sure he was lying. Who else fidgets like that?
Tuesday. She didn't talk to him at breakfast. She told Mummy he was a liar. Chetan's eyes filled with tears. "I didn't!" he said, but he still wouldn't look at her. Pooja took it as proof.
Friday. Their cousin Rohit, visiting from Pune, said casually over dinner, "Pooja, sorry about your headphones. I stepped on them on Sunday. I thought I'd told you."
Pooja put down her spoon. She looked at Chetan, who was still staring at his plate. He always looked like that when he was scared of being blamed.
"Chetan," she said quietly. "I'm sorry."

qa.q: Who actually broke Pooja's headphones?
qa.a: Their cousin Rohit said he stepped on them on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when Rohit admitted it?
qa.a: Pooja felt shocked and guilty, realising she had wrongly read Chetan's fidgeting as proof of lying.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Pooja do differently?
qa.a: She treated fidgeting and looking away as proof; next time she could ask calmly and look for facts before calling anyone a liar.

qa.q: What was it like for Chetan to be called a liar all week?
qa.a: Chetan felt hurt and scared, crying and staring at his plate because he was blamed for something he didn't do.

grounding: It shows a teenager believing fidgeting and averted eyes prove her brother lied, until the truth shows those cues were weak.

Vijay, you say you can always tell when your friends are lying? Let your Lavanya Nani, forty years a teacher, tell you about the first exam I ever invigilated.
There were two boys in the back row. One was shaking, wiping his hands on his trousers, looking everywhere except at me. The other sat calm as a lake. I was young and very sure of myself. I walked straight to the shaking boy and took his paper. "Where are the notes?"
There were no notes. He was just terrified of exams. His father had told him that if he failed he would be taken out of school.
The calm boy had the answers written on the inside of his shirt cuff. I found them only because he dropped his pen.
I apologised to the first boy in front of the whole class. And I never again trusted a trembling hand as proof of anything.

qa.q: Where did the calm boy have the answers written?
qa.a: On the inside of his shirt cuff.

qa.q: How did young Lavanya feel as she walked to the shaking boy?
qa.a: She felt confident and very sure of herself, believing his nervousness proved he was cheating.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Lavanya judged honesty?
qa.a: Finding the answers on the calm boy's cuff, after wrongly accusing the frightened one, showed her that nervous signs prove nothing.

qa.q: How might the shaking boy have felt when his paper was taken?
qa.a: He probably felt humiliated and even more frightened, already scared about failing and then wrongly accused.

grounding: A grandmother recalls wrongly reading a nervous student's trembling as proof of cheating, while the calm student was the one lying.

I'm Rafiq, and in my second year I learned something unpleasant about myself.
Our flat had three of us. Gurpreet was funny, confident, from my own town, great at cricket. Naresh was the quiet one who stammered and ate alone in his room.
When my phone charger and some cash went missing from my desk, Gurpreet shook his head sadly. "Bro, I saw Naresh in your room yesterday." I believed him instantly. Naresh went pale and tried to explain, but the words came out broken, and I didn't wait for them.
A week later, the building guard showed me the corridor camera. Gurpreet had gone into my room while I was at lectures. Naresh had only knocked to return my plate.
I still think about how quickly I trusted the charming one, the one like me, and how easily I doubted the awkward one. Charm told me nothing. I just liked it.

Subject: before you pay that agent

Dear Santosh,
I know you're excited about the job in Dubai, and I know the agent sounded wonderful on the phone. You said he knew everything, answered every question without a pause, and even cried a little talking about the workers he'd "helped." I believe he's good at talking. That's what worries me.
Last year, before I took my job, I stopped trusting how people sounded and started checking. Can you do the same?

If everything matches, wonderful. If he gets angry at questions, that tells you something too.
Don't send anything until we've checked it together this weekend.
Trisha

Ganga Di, the senior in the next room, stopped by again tonight. She read my story for the college magazine and said I'm the best writer she's seen in years. That I have "a real voice." That I remind her of herself.

In the Lisbon software office, Pablo sat two desks from Paulo, and by March he had noticed something.
"Your code is genius, man," Paulo said on Monday, leaning over Pablo's screen. "Honestly, you're the best developer on this floor." Pablo smiled. It felt good.
On Monday afternoon: "Hey, could you cover my weekend on-call?"
Two weeks later: "You're the only person here with real taste." Ten minutes later: "Could you review my pull request tonight? It's urgent."
Pablo started to notice the rhythm. The compliments were big and vague. They never mentioned anything specific he had actually done. And they always arrived just before a request.
His team lead, by contrast, had once written: "Your fix to the payment retry saved us a whole weekend." Nothing more. No request.
The next time Paulo called him a genius, Pablo just said, "Thanks. What do you need?" Paulo laughed awkwardly and told him.

qa.a: Pablo felt wary and a little let down, realising the flattering words were steering him toward favours.

qa.a: He thanked Paulo and asked directly what he needed, separating the compliment from the request.
